Excelente juego de plataformas de precisión. Su parecido mas fuerte a Super Meat Boy son los controles un poco imprecisos que le dan ese toque de inseguridad cada vez que saltas. 

Tiene 75 niveles y si tienes experiencia con otros juegos de plataforma mas o menos difíciles este juego sera extremadamente relajante (A excepción de algunos niveles que te dejaran pensando un rato).

Los boss fight son extremadamente faciles y no representan un reto como lo son los niveles finales. El Soundtrack es muy bueno y la experiencia visual es bastante estimulante. Arrojar tinta por todas partes para ir descubriendo la estructura del nivel es divertido. Aun con eso, si piensas que el gameplay es morirte para ir descubriendo el nivel estas EQUIVOCADO. Esto solo tiene sentido cuando lo juegas la primera vez. Puedes hacer uso del doble salto para arrojar tinta de forma segura. En menos de 5 horas pude hacer el 100% del juego.

Mi única queja es la falta de niveles adicionales. Siento que 75 niveles se queda corto y cuando llegue al Boss Fight Final me dio la sensación de que desbloquearía una segunda zona. Lo cierto es que ahí acaba el juego, es una lastima ya que las mecánicas son estimulantes. Bueno, también tengo otra queja pero esto es mas un Skill Issue: Las torretas disparan balas muy precisas, pareciera que te persiguen y saben exactamente donde vas a parar.


Los únicos logros complicados son completar el mundo 2 y el mundo 3 sin morir. El mundo 1 no es especialmente dificil pero puede frustrarte olvidar la estructura de algún nivel.

Recomiendo mucho este juego si quieres ampliar tu colección de juegos de plataforma de precisión. En mi opinión uno de los géneros mas desafiantes y estimulantes para jugar ya sea de forma tryhard o como una experiencia casual.

I'm not going to lie; I consider buying INK a gamble. For the first hour of playing it, I did not like this game. Much of what I will write in this review will be negative as well. Looking at the Steam achievement stats, only 8,8% of players finished the game, and only 35% even got past the first boss, which is 40 minutes into the game. There is a reason behind these numbers, mainly that this game is constructed around being difficult and has some mechanics and some level design that I would describe charitably as polarising. If you're new to platformer games, I would also give the advice to avoid this game like the plague.

And yet, I think the game managed to win me over in the end, if yet barely. Hopefully I will discover why below.

Let's start with the complaints. The first one is very subjective, because this game has very similar controls and movement mechanics to Super Meat Boy, and I hate them. You slide a lot on surfaces, accelerate quickly and carry a lot of momentum, which makes it a lot harder to correct your jumps and be precise. It also causes the game to be more punishing than the obstacles might lead you to believe. This makes levels of the game that focuses on precision platforming, as opposed to speed and pattern recognition, unbearable to me. Thing is, most of the precision-focused levels are gathered at the beginning of the game, which makes them the worst levels in the game in my eyes. 

There are also specific interactions I had a problem with, the worst one being the wall-jump. I have a habit of huddling against walls when there are projectiles in play. I don't think that's too unusual. However, if you're next to a wall in this game and then try to double-jump (something you often do to reveal the level, as it shoots out paint everywhere), it wall-jumps instead, even if you don't actually hold the directional button towards the wall. Before I realised this, I thought that the game was broken, randomly launching me off the map at bad moments. The game simply has some finicky mechanics like this, which increases the requirements of your inputs, and I think it makes the game needlessly difficult to control.

Add to this the level design. To describe it, I need only this example: In earlier levels, there are sections when you need to jump onto a platform above you. These platforms are shaped like boxes and placed directly above eachother, meaning that you need to use your double-jump to make a zigzag jump to stick to the side of the box above. Simple, right? Well, the developers for some reason placed these boxes far enough apart to require a pretty much flawless jump. If you miss, the momentum probably means that you can't correct in time to avoid death. And it's not just one jump: You need to do it several times in a row to beat the level. The fact that the space in between the boxes is made to barely give you room enough to make the jump is indicative of the entire game. Again, this game is made specifically to be difficult. Not always fun, but always difficult.

So why did I end up liking the game? Well, part of me thinks that it's simply commitment bias. I did end up being one of the 8,8% finishing the game, after all. But the game also shines in sections that require fast execution and pattern recognition instead of precision platforming. Obstacle courses, not balancing acts. And the game does turn more into this direction as the game goes on. While lucking out on making the exact jumps I needed to make in the earlier levels, I felt nothing but a slight sense of relief that I wouldn't have to do it again. In contrast, I actually felt like I slowly understood the later levels, what to do and how; like I was actually thinking. And when you blast through one of those levels, especially when you manage to do it at high speed, it is really fun. As a result, I felt satisfied at the end, even if I couldn't forget the bad parts of the game.

In conclusion, I wouldn't blame you if you skipped INK. It is brutal and I think the earlier levels are dreadful. It surely isn't for everyone. However, if you liked Super Meat Boy, if you like hardcore platformers, if you're used to die in games and find the grind enjoyable, then I can't say that there isn't some fun to be had here. I don't regret having played it.

A really cool platformer with 75 levels including 4 tutorial levels and 3 bosses. The levels are rather short and if you're not completely terrible at platforming, they can be completed in under 2h.

The main appeal of the game is obviously the visuals. Levels are completely empty until you splatter them with colorful ink and uncover their geometry. The goal is always to reach the exit, but sometimes it has to be opened by destroying all enemies in the level. There are spikes, projectiles, moving blocks that can squish you and an abyss below that can lead to your demise. Dying always causes a small ink explosion, revealing more of the level and thus helping you progress towards finishing it.

The platforming itself is not too difficult once you revealed the level. It only gets a little tricky towards the end, when homing projectile shooters are introduced, but never gets even remotely close to, say, Super Meat Boy levels. 
Speaking of which, the game feels a lot like Super Meat Boy in terms of character movement and control. Your little square is very fast, slidy and floaty, which may take some time getting used to, especially for casual players and platformer newbies. 
If you're looking for a greater challenge, you can attempt the achievements for beating one third, i.e. 25 levels of the game in sequence without dying. They're actually quite difficult as all levels are invisible on your first attempt, so you need to know them by heart.

The music is a beautiful and calming electronic ambient soundtrack, that fits the game perfectly and never feels repetitive or annoying.

Lastly, have a look at the achievement names. So many ink puns. Beautiful, just like the rest of the game.

"INK" est facile à décrire: c'est un hardcore platformer à la "[b]Super Meat Boy[/b]", mais avec une ambition et un prix de "petit jeu" (tout y est très simple et géométrique), et avec un gimmick franchement sympathique - dans "INK", le décor est invisible jusqu'à être aspergé d'encre, ce qui se produit par simple contact avec notre héros (un carré blanc) ou avec ses ennemis, ou en projetant de l'encre lors d'un double saut, ou en mourant à proximité d'une paroi.

Ce gimmick est important pendant la première moitié de l'expérience et fournit des sensations originales et agréables: on aurait pu croire que le décor invisible causerait de l'agacement ou des erreurs injustes, mais le level design est parfaitement conçu, très intuitif, et joue beaucoup sur le plaisir de la découverte. L'effet est visuellement très réussi et le jeu, malgré ses formes basiques, devient franchement beau grâce à cette superposition continue de couleurs. En plus de la progression dans les trois mondes du jeu (chacun avec 24 niveaux plus un combat de boss, pour 75 niveaux en tout), on pourra aussi s'amuser à dénicher vingt pièces marquées d'un cœur: cet objectif annexe est malin, la plupart des pièces (elles aussi invisibles et devant être aspergées) sont cachées logiquement et de façon satisfaisante.

Passé la seconde moitié du jeu, le gimmick de "INK" perd beaucoup de pertinence puisque les ennemis, les projectiles et les morts s'accumulent et le décor devient donc visible bien plus vite, mais le jeu reste un très bon hardcore platformer, et je me suis régalé jusqu'au bout. Des joueurs se sont plaints d'une maniabilité un petit peu raide et de la difficulté du troisième monde, mais à mon avis, la maniabilité est justement un des points forts de "INK" (sa raideur fait partie du défi, le level design est conçu autour), et j'ai beaucoup aimé la difficulté extrême de la fin, parfaitement dosée à mon avis.

J'ai gagné "INK" à 100% en quatre heures avec l'essentiel de ses succès (qui sont bien pensés, je ne compte ceci dit pas essayer les trois derniers qui exigent chacun de gagner un monde sans mourir), j'ai passé un très bon moment et je recommande "INK" à tous les amateurs de hardcore platformers.
